parts.label: (a)
key_concepts: relation between charge, p.d. and current
hints: Hint 1: Start by thinking about what the current in the circuit is doing to the charge stored on the capacitor plates as time passes.
Hint 2: Next think about how the p.d. across the capacitor, which is also the p.d. across the resistor in this loop, changes as that charge falls.
Hint 3: Finally link the resistor p.d. to the current through it, and explain why the current falls quickly at first and then more and more slowly.
parts.proper_answer: As charge $Q$ leaves the capacitor, $V = Q/C$ falls so p.d. across resistor falls. By $V = IR$, current $I$ falls proportionally to $Q$. Since $I$ is the rate of loss of $Q$, the rate of decrease itself decreases, giving an exponential decay of $I$ with $t$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What Drives the Current**
You have a charged capacitor connected only to a resistor once the switch closes. There is no battery. The energy and push for current comes entirely from the charge already on the plates. As current flows, positive charge leaves one plate and arrives at the other, so the stored charge $Q$ decreases with time.

Step 2: **From Charge to p.d. to Current**
For a capacitor, p.d. is proportional to charge: $$V_C = \frac{Q}{C}$$ So as $Q$ falls, $V_C$ falls. In this single loop the capacitor p.d. must equal the resistor p.d., so $V_R$ also falls. For the resistor, current is proportional to p.d.: $$V_R = I R$$ So as $V_R$ falls, $I$ must fall in the same proportion.

Step 3: **Why the Curve Flattens Out**
But $I$ is itself the rate at which $Q$ is lost. So a smaller $I$ means $Q$ is now being lost more slowly, which means $V$ then falls more slowly, which means $I$ then falls more slowly. This feedback gives the characteristic discharge shape: steep fall at first when $Q$ and $I$ are large, then ever gentler slope, tending to zero - exponential decay.

parts.label: (b)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Focus on the instant $t = 0$ just after the switch is closed. What is the full 12 V p.d. across at that moment, and therefore across the resistor?
Hint 2: Read the initial current $I_0$ at $t = 0$ from Fig. 6.2 in mA, convert it to A, then use resistance = p.d. / current.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Use the $t = 0$ Condition**
At $t = 0$ the capacitor is still fully charged to $12\text{ V}$. The moment the switch closes, this whole p.d. appears across $R$ because they are in parallel in the loop: $$V_{R0} = V_{C0} = 12\text{ V}$$

Step 2: **Read $I_0$ and Apply $R = V/I$**
From Fig. 6.2, extrapolate the curve back to $t = 0$: $$I_0 \approx 0.13\text{ mA} = 0.13 \times 10^{-3}\text{ A}$$ Then: $$R = \frac{V_{R0}}{I_0} = \frac{12}{0.13 \times 10^{-3}} \approx 9.2 \times 10^4\, \Omega$$ This is about $92\text{ k}\Omega$.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: Recall what the time constant $\tau$ means on an $I$-$t$ discharge graph - the time for the current to fall to about 37% of its starting value.
Hint 2: Calculate $0.37 \times I_0$ using your $I_0 \approx 0.13\text{ mA}$ from (b)(i), then find on Fig. 6.2 the time where the current has that value.
Hint 3: Alternatively pick any clear $(I,t)$ pair from the curve and substitute into $I = I_0 \exp(-t/\tau)$ to solve for $\tau$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What $\tau$ Means**
For discharge: $$I = I_0 \exp\left(-\frac{t}{\tau}\right)$$ When $t = \tau$, $$I = I_0 \exp(-1) = \frac{I_0}{e} \approx 0.37 I_0$$ So you just need the time for the current to drop to 37% of its initial value.

Step 2: **Find the 37% Current**
With $I_0 \approx 0.13\text{ mA}$: $$I(\tau) \approx 0.37 \times 0.13 \approx 0.048\text{ mA}$$ Go across Fig. 6.2 at $I = 0.048\text{ mA}$ (about 4.8 divisions up if 0.01 mA per small square) and read down to $t$.

Step 3: **Read Off $\tau$**
The curve reaches $\approx 0.048\text{ mA}$ at: $$\tau \approx 4.2 \text{ to } 4.4\text{ s} \approx 4.3\text{ s}$$ Any correct pair substituted into the exponential equation gives the same result.

parts.label: (c)
hints: Hint 1: Remember how the time constant links the two circuit components $R$ and $C$ together in one simple product.
Hint 2: Rearrange that relation to make $C$ the subject and substitute your values of $\tau$ from (b)(ii) and $R$ from (b)(i), keeping $R$ in ohms and $\tau$ in seconds.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Use $\tau = RC$**
The time constant for a resistor-capacitor discharge is: $$\tau = R C$$ This makes sense: larger $R$ limits current so discharge is slower, larger $C$ stores more charge so takes longer.

Step 2: **Calculate $C$**
Rearrange: $$C = \frac{\tau}{R}$$ Substitute: $$C = \frac{4.3}{9.2 \times 10^4} \approx 4.7 \times 10^{-5}\text{ F}$$ That is about $47\, \mu\text{F}$, to 2 significant figures with unit farad.
